The greatest area is 81 and the least is 45, so the difference is 36. I found these by treating each interior point as a "dent" cut out of the square and checking which dent combinations give a simple hexagon.

**Setup.** The four corners (0,0), (10,0), (10,10), (0,10) form a square of area 100. The interior points are P = (3,4) and Q = (6,2). In a simple hexagon the corners stay in square order, and each interior point is inserted into the boundary. The hexagon's area is 100 minus the dent areas.

**Dent areas.** If a point is inserted alone into one edge, the dent is the triangle on that edge with the point as apex.

| Edge | P = (3,4) | Q = (6,2) |
|---|---|---|
| Bottom | 20 | 10 |
| Right | 35 | 20 |
| Top | 30 | 40 |
| Left | 15 | 30 |

If both points are inserted into the same edge, the dent is a quadrilateral. Only the orderings that give a simple polygon count.

| Edge | Valid ordering | Dent area |
|---|---|---|
| Bottom | (0,0), P, Q, (10,0) | 19 |
| Left | (0,0), P, Q, (0,10) | 21 |
| Right | (10,0), Q, P, (10,10) | 36 |
| Top | (10,10), Q, P, (0,10) | 46 |

The other ordering on each edge self-intersects.

**Minimum dent.** The smallest dent on separate edges is P on the left plus Q on the bottom, which is 25. The same-edge bottom case gives 19, which is smaller. The hexagon is (0,0), P, Q, (10,0), (10,10), (0,10), so a_max = 100 − 19 = 81.

**Maximum dent.** Several larger pairs fail because their triangles overlap or cross:
- P on the right with Q on the top (75) overlaps at the shared corner (10,10).
- P on the right with Q on the left (65) has crossing edges.
- P on the top with Q on the left (60) overlaps at (0,10).
- P on the bottom with Q on the top (60) has crossing edges.

The largest valid pair is P on the left (15) with Q on the top (40), giving 55. The two triangles share only the corner (0,10) and do not overlap. The next best valid options are 50 (P top, Q right) and 46 (same-edge top), so a_min = 100 − 55 = 45.

**Result.** a_max − a_min = 81 − 45 = 36.

ANSWER: 36
